extracted.intended_audience: British legislators, statesmen, and the politically-engaged reading public (late 18th-century/educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance on how to form, preserve, and administer a free and stable government—emphasizing fiscal prudence, respect for property, tempering liberty with restraint, and cautious reform. Aimed at political actors and citizens deciding constitutional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a balance between acquisition and state demands
rubrics_metrics.description: "To keep a balance between the power of acquisition on the part of the subject and the demands he is to answer on the part of the state is the fundamental part of the skill of a true politician."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Means of acquisition are prior; good order is the foundation of all good things. The populace must be tractable and obedient without servility; magistrates must command reverence and laws authority. Policy should preserve incentives to industry rather than unsettle them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect property and preserve industry
rubrics_metrics.description: "They must respect that property of which they cannot partake... Of this consolation whoever deprives them deadens their industry, and strikes at the root of all acquisition as of all conservation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undermining belief in just outcomes or confiscating accumulated fortunes destroys industry and harms the poor most. Protecting property (even property some cannot share) sustains labor, acquisition, and social stability; the opposite makes rulers 'cruel oppressors'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue must not be trifled with; fiscal prudence is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: "The revenue will not be trifled with. The prattling about the rights of men will not be accepted in payment of a biscuit or a pound of gunpowder... To tell the people that they are relieved by the dilapidation of their public estate is a cruel and insolent imposition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposed fiscal measures for real effect on public supplies and services. Beware rhetorical claims of 'relief' that are actually destruction of public revenue (examples in text: paper circulation schemes, coining church bells). Policy must secure actual resources for necessities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial contrivances only work on a settled order
rubrics_metrics.description: "Too many of the financiers by profession are apt to see nothing in revenue but banks, and circulations, and annuities... They are good, but then only good when they assume the effects of that settled order, and are built upon it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruments like banks, annuities, tontines are useful only when founded on stable institutions and secure property; using them to paper over the collapse of public order is dangerous and short-sighted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether 'relief' measures genuinely benefit the people
rubrics_metrics.description: "Statesmen... ought first to have carefully attended to the solution of this problem:--Whether it be more advantageous to the people to pay considerably and to gain in proportion, or to gain little or nothing and to be disburdened of all contribution?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers must weigh trade-offs between taxation with benefits versus nominal 'liberation' that leaves people with less. Do not accept facile claims that destruction of revenue equals popular relief; analyze net effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty must be tempered by wisdom and virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: "But what is liberty without wisdom and without virtue? It is the greatest of all possible evils; for it is folly, vice, and madness, without tuition or restraint."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberty left unguided by moral instruction and institutional restraint leads to chaos. Political reform must combine freedom with education, virtue, and structures that prevent license and degradation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming a free government requires sagacious, combining minds
rubrics_metrics.description: "To form a free government... requires much thought, deep reflection, a sagacious, powerful, and combining mind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giving freedom or setting up government superficially is easy; the hard task is balancing liberty and restraint into a durable constitution. Leadership requires depth, foresight, and capacity to integrate competing elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pandering to popularity; do not become 'bidders at an auction of popularity'
rubrics_metrics.description: "When the leaders choose to make themselves bidders at an auction of popularity, their talents, in the construction of the state, will be of no service. They will become flatterers instead of legislators."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political actors who compete on spectacle and ever-more-popular concessions will outbid moderation, stigmatize compromise, and undermine the ability to later temper and govern. Leaders should preserve credibility to moderate when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer preservation and cautious alteration of constitutional inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: "I would make the reparation as nearly as possible in the style of the building... Let us preserve what they have left; and standing on the firm ground of the British Constitution, let us be satisfied to admire, rather than attempt to follow in their desperate flights."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reform should aim to conserve salutary institutions and repair by analogy to existing structures; emulate ancestors' prudence and avoid wholesale destruction in the name of novelty. Change should serve preservation, not radical invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be suspicious of revolutionary maxim 'everything must be destroyed and recreated'
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation of Rabaut de St. Étienne: "...tout détruire; oui, tout détruire; puisque tout est à récréer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unrestrained zeal to overturn all establishments risks removing useful functions and producing poverty and social ruin; reforms must discriminate between genuine grievances and needless demolition of social supports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand financial accountability and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that large aggregate public charges and vague account items provoked no inquiry in the Assembly (discussion of M. de Calonne's accounts and the mysterious large 'subsistances' item).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public expenditures should be itemized and scrutinized; secret or aggregated charges breed suspicion and enable misuse. Fiscal oversight is a political necessity to understand the real state of the nation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not allow 'liberty' rhetoric to excuse incapacity or crime
rubrics_metrics.description: "The effects of the incapacity shown by the popular leaders... are to be covered with the 'all-atoning name' of Liberty... But what is liberty without wisdom and without virtue?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of acting in liberty's name must be tested against competence and moral conduct. Leaders cannot hide destructive policies or violent deeds behind high-sounding language; rhetoric is not a substitute for sound governance.
